{{Short description|Method to calculate trajectory calculations for spacecraft}}
In [[astrodynamics]], the '''patched conic approximation''' or '''patched two-body approximation'''<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Roger |first1=R. Bate |author-link1=Roger R. Bate |last2=Mueller |first2=Donald D. |last3=White |first3=Jerry E. |year=1971 |title=Fundamentals of Astrodynamics |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofas00bate |url-access=registration |series=Dover Books on Astronomy and Astrophysics |location=New York |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=0486600610 |lccn=73157430}}</ref><ref>Lagerstrom, P. A. and Kevorkian, J. [1963], ''Earth-to-moon trajectories in the restricted three-body problem'', Journal de mecanique, p. 189-218.</ref> is a method to simplify [[trajectory]] calculations for [[spacecraft]] in a multiple-body environment.

==Method==

The simplification is achieved by dividing space into various parts by assigning each of the ''n'' bodies (e.g. the [[Sun]], [[planets]], [[moons]]) its own [[sphere of influence (astrodynamics)|sphere of influence]]. When the spacecraft is within the sphere of influence of a smaller body, only the [[gravitational force]] between the spacecraft and that smaller body is considered, otherwise the gravitational force between the spacecraft and the larger body is used. This reduces a complicated [[n-body problem]] to multiple [[two-body problem]]s, for which the solutions are the well-known [[conic sections]] of the [[Kepler orbit]]s.

Although this method gives a good approximation of trajectories for [[interplanetary spaceflight|interplanetary]] spacecraft missions, there are missions for which this approximation does not provide sufficiently accurate results.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Koon |first1=Wang Sang |last2=Loo |first2=Martin W. |last3=Marsden |first3=Jerrold E. |author-link3=Jerrold E. Marsden |last4=Ross |first4=Shane D. |year=2011 |orig-year=2005 |title=Dynamical Systems, the Three-Body Problem and Space Mission Design |url=http://www.dept.aoe.vt.edu/~sdross/books/KoLoMaRo_DMissionBook_2011-04-25.pdf |version=v1.2 |publisher=Marsden Books |page=5|isbn=978-0-615-24095-4}}</ref> Notably, it does not model [[Lagrangian point]]s.

=== Mathematical formulation ===

In the patched conic approximation, the spacecraft trajectory is modeled as a sequence of two-body problems. Within the sphere of influence of a body with [[Standard gravitational parameter|gravitational parameter]] <math>\mu</math>, the spacecraft motion satisfies:<math display="block">\ddot{\mathbf{r}} = -\frac{\mu}{r^3}\mathbf{r}</math>The solution in each region is a conic section (elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic), which can be expressed using classical [[orbital elements]] or state vectors. At the boundary between spheres of influence, the trajectory segments are "patched" by enforcing continuity of position and velocity:<math display="block">\mathbf{r}_- = \mathbf{r}_+, \qquad \mathbf{v}_- = \mathbf{v}_+</math>For example, when departing a planet, the spacecraft follows a hyperbolic escape trajectory with hyperbolic excess velocity <math>\mathbf{v}_\infty</math>. This velocity is then used as the initial condition for the heliocentric trajectory:<math display="block">\mathbf{v}_{\text{helio}} = \mathbf{v}_{\text{planet}} + \mathbf{v}_\infty</math>This process is repeated at each sphere of influence boundary to construct an approximate multi-body trajectory.

==Example: Earth-to-Mars transfer==

On an [[Earth]]-to-[[Mars]] transfer, a [[hyperbolic trajectory]] is required to escape from Earth's [[gravity well]], then an [[elliptic orbit|elliptic]] or [[hyperbolic trajectory|hyperbolic]] trajectory in the Sun's sphere of influence is required to transfer from Earth's sphere of influence to that of Mars, etc. By patching these conic sections together—matching the position and velocity vectors between segments—the appropriate mission trajectory can be found.

=== Numerical example ===
A simple Earth-to-Mars patched conic calculation can be made by assuming circular, coplanar planetary orbits and a [[Hohmann transfer orbit]] between the mean orbital radii of Earth and Mars.<ref name=":0" /> Let<math display="block">
r_E = 1.496\times 10^8\ \text{km}, \qquad
r_M = 2.279\times 10^8\ \text{km}, \qquad
\mu_\odot = 1.327\times 10^{11}\ \text{km}^3/\text{s}^2
</math>The [[Semi-major and semi-minor axes|semi-major axis]] of the heliocentric transfer ellipse is<math display="block">
a_t = \frac{r_E+r_M}{2} = 1.888\times 10^8\ \text{km}
</math>The circular heliocentric speeds of Earth and Mars are<math display="block">
v_E = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_\odot}{r_E}} = 29.8\ \text{km/s},
\qquad
v_M = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_\odot}{r_M}} = 24.1\ \text{km/s}
</math>Using the [[vis-viva equation]], the spacecraft speed on the transfer ellipse at Earth's orbit is<math display="block">
v_{t,E} =
\sqrt{\mu_\odot\left(\frac{2}{r_E}-\frac{1}{a_t}\right)}
= 32.7\ \text{km/s}
</math>For this tangential, prograde transfer, the required Earth departure hyperbolic excess speed is<math display="block">
v_{\infty,E} = v_{t,E}-v_E = 2.94\ \text{km/s}
</math>In the patched conic approximation, this quantity becomes the hyperbolic excess speed of the Earth departure hyperbola. If the spacecraft departs from a circular low Earth parking orbit with radius <math>r_p=6,578\ \text{km}</math>, then the required impulsive burn is approximately<math display="block">
\Delta v_E =
\sqrt{v_{\infty,E}^2+\frac{2\mu_E}{r_p}}
-
\sqrt{\frac{\mu_E}{r_p}}
= 3.61\ \text{km/s}
</math>where <math>\mu_E = 398,600\ \text{km}^3/\text{s}^2</math>. At Mars, the spacecraft speed on the transfer ellipse is<math display="block">
v_{t,M} =
\sqrt{\mu_\odot\left(\frac{2}{r_M}-\frac{1}{a_t}\right)}
= 21.5\ \text{km/s}
</math>For this tangential transfer, the Mars arrival hyperbolic excess speed is the magnitude of the difference between Mars's circular speed and the transfer orbit speed<math display="block">
v_{\infty,M} = v_M-v_{t,M} = 2.65\ \text{km/s}
</math>This becomes the hyperbolic excess speed of the Mars arrival hyperbola. For insertion into a circular orbit 200 km above Mars, taking <math>r_p = 3,596\ \text{km}</math> and <math>\mu_M=42,828\ \text{km}^3/\text{s}^2</math>, the approximate capture burn is<math display="block">
\Delta v_M =
\sqrt{v_{\infty,M}^2+\frac{2\mu_M}{r_p}}
-
\sqrt{\frac{\mu_M}{r_p}}
= 2.10\ \text{km/s}
</math>The heliocentric time of flight for the Hohmann transfer is half the [[Orbital period|period of the transfer ellipse]]:<math display="block">
t = \pi\sqrt{\frac{a_t^3}{\mu_\odot}}
= 2.24\times 10^7\ \text{s}
\approx 259\ \text{days}
</math>
